record.paper_title: Logical connections between some open problems concerning nil rings
record.original_question: Let R be a ring such that for every x, y in R there exists an integer n with (xy − yx)^n = 0. Do the nilpotent elements of R form an ideal?

evidence.quote: P4 (Herstein [3]) If for every element x and y of a ring R we have (xy − yx)^n = 0 for some n, do the nilpotent elements of R form an ideal?

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Let $R$ be an associative (not necessarily unital) ring with the property that for every pair of elements $x,y \in R$ there exists a positive integer $n = n(x,y)$ such that
$$(xy - yx)^n = 0.$$
That is, every additive commutator in $R$ is nilpotent. Let $N(R) = \{a \in R : a^k = 0 \text{ for some positive integer } k\}$ denote the set of nilpotent elements of $R$.

Must $N(R)$ be a (two-sided) ideal of $R$?
artifact.status_search_result: This is a classical question of Herstein, often listed alongside the Köthe conjecture among open problems concerning nil rings. Searches do not turn up a published solution; surveys on nil rings and commutativity conditions continue to discuss related problems but do not record a resolution. The status appears to be still open.

status_evidence.title: Nil ideal - Wikipedia
status_evidence.snippet: For a non-commutative ring, it is not in general true that the set of nilpotent elements forms an ideal... Nil ideals are still associated with interesting open questions, especially the unsolved Köthe conjecture.
status_evidence.claim: The set of nilpotent elements need not form an ideal in general, and questions about when it does remain connected to open problems.

status_evidence.title: Commutativity conditions for rings: 1950–2005
status_evidence.snippet: Much of the initial thrust of the work in this area was either authored by Herstein or inspired by his work.
status_evidence.claim: Herstein-style commutator/nilpotence problems form an active and longstanding area, with several questions still unresolved.
